option_description: Controls whether per-protocol access control lists for SMB (TCP 445), NFS (TCP/UDP 2049), and iSCSI (TCP 3260) are enforced at zone boundary firewalls or VLAN ACL enforcement points to restrict storage session initiation to authorized source zones only.
security_impact: The Rego policy triggers the permissive_storage_protocol_ingress_filtering exposure when this is false AND either nas_vlan_isolation_enforced is false or unauthorized_zone_storage_access_observed is true. Without per-protocol ACLs, hosts from DMZ, guest, or other untrusted VLANs can initiate storage sessions directly against the NAS, bypassing zone boundary controls entirely.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Query firewall ACL rules for NAS-bound storage protocol ports on Cisco ASA or IOS-based firewalls to verify source-zone restrictions.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: ACL entries explicitly permitting SMB/NFS/iSCSI only from named trusted source IP ranges or VLAN interfaces, with a deny-all default.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Review VLAN ACLs on a Cisco Catalyst Layer 3 switch to verify that VACL or RACL entries restrict storage protocols to authorized VLANs.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Named ACLs with permit statements scoped to authorized source VLAN subnets and an implicit or explicit deny for all other sources.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Inspect the firewall policy configuration file for an iptables-based Linux firewall acting as the zone boundary device.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: ACCEPT rules scoped to specific source IP ranges for storage ports, followed by DROP or REJECT rules for all other sources.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Navigate to the firewall zone policy configuration in a GUI-based NGFW such as Palo Alto Networks to verify storage protocol application rules.
how_to_obtain.navigation: Panorama or Device Web UI > Policies > Security > Filter by Destination Zone matching NAS segment > Verify Application columns show 'smb', 'nfs', 'iscsi' with Source Zone restricted to authorized storage client zone.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Policy rules explicitly name storage applications and restrict source zones to approved zones, with no any-to-any or untrusted-zone rules matching storage ports.

typical_values: false (common in flat or legacy environments where storage VLANs are trusted by default)
true (expected in segmented environments with explicit storage zone firewall policies)

option_description: Indicates whether evidence exists in firewall logs, NAS access logs, or network flow data of storage protocol sessions (SMB, NFS, iSCSI) initiated from hosts residing in untrusted or adjacent zones that are not authorized to access the NAS.
security_impact: The Rego policy triggers permissive_storage_protocol_ingress_filtering when this is true in combination with either missing ACLs or missing VLAN isolation. Observed unauthorized access confirms that current zone boundary controls are insufficient and that active cross-zone storage session traversal is occurring, representing confirmed exploitation of the boundary weakness.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Analyze NAS audit logs on a Linux-based NAS or Samba server for authentication or connection events sourced from IP addresses outside authorized client subnets.
how_to_obtain.command: grep -E '(smbd|nfsd|iscsi)' /var/log/syslog | awk '{print $NF}' | grep -v '<authorized_subnet>' | sort | uniq -c | sort -rn
how_to_obtain.expected_output: No entries from unauthorized source IPs; any results indicate active unauthorized zone access.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Use NetFlow or sFlow data aggregated in a collector to identify flows on storage ports sourced from non-authorized VLANs using nfdump.
how_to_obtain.command: nfdump -R /var/netflow/ -n 20 -s srcip/bytes 'port 445 or port 2049 or port 3260' | grep -vE '<authorized_cidr>'
how_to_obtain.expected_output: No flow records from unauthorized source IP ranges; presence of flows from DMZ or guest subnets confirms the attribute should be set to true.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Query firewall connection logs for established sessions to NAS IP addresses on storage ports where source IP belongs to untrusted zones.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Source IPs matching only authorized client subnets; any DMZ, guest, or unclassified source IPs confirm unauthorized zone access.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Attempt a probe connection to NAS storage ports from a host in an adjacent or untrusted VLAN to empirically verify whether zone boundary controls block access.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: All ports show 'filtered' status from untrusted VLAN source; 'open' results confirm unauthorized zone access is possible and attribute should be true.

typical_values: false (desired state; no unauthorized zone access confirmed)
true (indicates active or historical cross-zone storage access requiring immediate remediation)

option_description: Controls whether the NAS device resides in a dedicated VLAN segment with Layer 2 and Layer 3 isolation ensuring that inter-VLAN communication to the NAS requires traversal of a stateful firewall or enforced ACL, preventing direct reachability from untrusted or adjacent VLANs.
security_impact: The Rego policy triggers permissive_storage_protocol_ingress_filtering when this is false AND either storage_protocol_zone_acls_configured is false or unauthorized_zone_storage_access_observed is true. Without VLAN isolation, any host on a Layer 3 switch with open inter-VLAN routing can reach the NAS directly on storage protocol ports, making ACL-based controls the only line of defense.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Verify the VLAN assignment of NAS switch ports and check for inter-VLAN routing policies on Cisco Catalyst switches.
how_to_obtain.command: show interfaces trunk | grep -A2 <NAS_port>; show ip route <NAS_subnet>
how_to_obtain.expected_output: NAS ports assigned to a dedicated storage VLAN ID not shared with other zones; routing to NAS subnet traverses a firewall next-hop rather than a directly connected SVI.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Check for routed SVIs on the storage VLAN and verify that ACLs are applied to restrict inter-VLAN forwarding on the Layer 3 switch.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: SVI for NAS VLAN shows an ip access-group statement referencing an inbound ACL, or the SVI is absent and routing is handled by a firewall.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Review VLAN topology and inter-VLAN routing configuration in the network management platform such as Cisco DNA Center or SolarWinds Network Topology.
how_to_obtain.navigation: Network Management Platform > Topology > Select NAS switch > VLAN Details > Verify NAS ports are in dedicated VLAN with no shared membership to untrusted VLANs > Check inter-VLAN routing paths.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: NAS VLAN shown as isolated with inter-VLAN routing paths traversing a firewall device rather than direct Layer 3 forwarding on the switch.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Perform a traceroute from a host in an adjacent VLAN to the NAS IP to verify a firewall hop exists in the path rather than direct Layer 3 switching.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Path shows a firewall IP as the first hop rather than a Layer 3 switch SVI gateway, confirming inter-VLAN traffic traverses a firewall enforcement point.

typical_values: false (common in environments where NAS is placed in a shared server VLAN without dedicated segmentation)
true (expected in environments with a dedicated storage VLAN and firewall-enforced inter-VLAN routing)

option_description: Controls whether NFS exports apply root_squash or all_squash directives to remap client-supplied UID and GID values to a restricted anonymous user, preventing NFS clients from presenting arbitrary UNIX identity credentials when accessing the export.
security_impact: The Rego policy triggers nfs_trust_propagation_via_uid_gid_mapping when this is false AND nfs_export_crosses_trust_zone_boundary is true AND nfs_auth_mechanism is 'sys' or 'none'. Without squashing, a client in a lower-trust zone can set their local UID to 0 or any privileged UID and present that identity to the NFS server, achieving unauthorized privilege escalation across the trust zone boundary.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Inspect the NFS exports configuration file for the presence and scope of squash directives on each export.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Each export line contains 'root_squash' or 'all_squash' in the options field, for example: /data/share 192.168.10.0/24(rw,sync,root_squash)

how_to_obtain.instruction: Use exportfs to display the currently active NFS export configuration including squash options as seen by the running NFS daemon.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Output lists each export with options including 'root_squash' or 'all_squash'; absence of these options or presence of 'no_root_squash' indicates squashing is disabled.

how_to_obtain.instruction: On enterprise NAS appliances such as NetApp ONTAP, verify NFS export policy rules for squash settings using the CLI.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: The 'anon' field shows '65534' (nobody) and rule options include squash configuration; a value of '0' in the anon field indicates root squashing is not applied.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Review NFS export settings through the NAS vendor web management interface to verify squash configuration per share.
how_to_obtain.navigation: NAS Admin Console > Shared Folders > NFS Shares > Select Share > Edit > Advanced Options > Verify 'Root Squash' or 'All Squash' is enabled.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Root Squash or All Squash option is checked/enabled for each export accessible to cross-zone clients.

typical_values: true with root_squash (default on most Linux NFS servers; prevents root identity propagation but allows other UIDs)
false with no_root_squash (commonly seen in misconfigured or legacy NFS servers, particularly in HPC or application-specific deployments)
true with all_squash (most restrictive; maps all client UIDs to anonymous; less common due to operational overhead)

option_description: Indicates whether any NFS export is configured to allow client access from hosts residing in a lower trust zone than the NFS server itself, as determined by comparing the export client list against the network zone topology.
security_impact: The Rego policy triggers nfs_trust_propagation_via_uid_gid_mapping when this is true AND nfs_auth_mechanism is 'sys' or 'none' AND nfs_uid_gid_squashing_enabled is false. Cross-zone NFS exports combined with AUTH_SYS authentication are the critical precondition for trust propagation attacks, as untrusted clients can send arbitrary UID/GID claims that the server accepts without cryptographic validation.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Extract allowed client IP ranges from the NFS exports file and cross-reference against network zone topology documentation to identify any clients in lower-trust zones.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: All client IP ranges belong to the same or higher trust zone as the NFS server; any ranges matching DMZ, guest, or lower-classification subnets indicate a trust zone boundary crossing.

how_to_obtain.instruction: On NetApp ONTAP, list NFS export policy rules and compare client match fields against zone topology to identify cross-zone exports.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: clientmatch fields show only trusted zone subnets; any DMZ or untrusted subnet in clientmatch fields confirms the export crosses a trust boundary.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Review network zone topology documentation and cross-reference with the NFS export client list to formally determine whether any permitted clients reside in lower-trust zones.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: A mapping document confirming all NFS client ranges are in zones of equal or higher trust than the NFS server; any exceptions indicate this attribute should be set to true.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Attempt to mount the NFS export from a host in an adjacent or lower-trust VLAN to empirically verify whether cross-zone NFS mounting is possible.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Mount attempt fails with 'access denied' from lower-trust zone host; successful mount confirms the export crosses the trust zone boundary.

typical_values: false (desired state; NFS exports restricted to clients within the same trust zone)
true (commonly observed in organizations with flat NFS architectures or legacy application dependencies on cross-zone NFS mounts)

option_description: Specifies the authentication and security flavor used by NFS exports to validate client identity. Options range from AUTH_SYS (no cryptographic validation, relies on client-supplied UID/GID) through Kerberos variants providing cryptographic authentication (krb5), integrity protection (krb5i), and full encryption with privacy (krb5p).
security_impact: The Rego policy triggers nfs_trust_propagation_via_uid_gid_mapping when this value is 'sys' or 'none' AND nfs_export_crosses_trust_zone_boundary is true AND nfs_uid_gid_squashing_enabled is false. AUTH_SYS provides no cryptographic proof of client identity, meaning any client can fabricate UID/GID values. Using 'none' is the most severe case, providing no authentication whatsoever at the zone boundary.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Inspect the /etc/exports file for sec= directives on each export to determine the configured authentication flavor.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Export options include 'sec=krb5', 'sec=krb5i', or 'sec=krb5p'; absence of any sec= directive means the default of 'sec=sys' (AUTH_SYS) is in effect.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Query the running NFS daemon statistics and active mount options to confirm the negotiated security flavor in use by active clients.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Mount options show 'sec=krb5p' or equivalent Kerberos flavor; 'sec=sys' in output confirms AUTH_SYS is the active mechanism.

how_to_obtain.instruction: On NetApp ONTAP, display NFS export policy rules with security flavor configuration for each policy rule.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: rorule and rwrule fields show 'krb5', 'krb5i', or 'krb5p'; values of 'sys' or 'any' indicate AUTH_SYS or unauthenticated access is permitted.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Use rpcinfo to query the NFS server for supported security flavors and confirm whether Kerberos GSS flavors are advertised.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: GSS/Kerberos security flavors listed in server capabilities; absence of Kerberos flavor listings confirms only AUTH_SYS is supported.

typical_values: sys (overwhelmingly common default; most Linux and NAS deployments use AUTH_SYS without explicit configuration)
krb5p (seen in high-security environments with Active Directory Kerberos integration, particularly government and financial sectors)
krb5i (moderate use in environments requiring integrity but not full encryption overhead)
none (rare but observed in legacy or development NFS mounts; represents complete absence of authentication)

option_description: Controls whether NAS management interfaces including HTTP/S admin consoles, SNMP, and SSH are accessible exclusively via a dedicated out-of-band management VLAN or network segment that is physically or logically isolated from the data-plane storage client network.
security_impact: The Rego policy triggers management_plane_zone_colocation when this is false AND either management_interfaces_exposed_on_data_vlan is true or acl_restricts_mgmt_access_to_admin_hosts_only is absent. Without a dedicated OOB management network, a compromised storage client host can reach NAS management interfaces directly from the data VLAN, enabling lateral movement to the management plane and full NAS compromise from a storage client position.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Inspect NAS network interface configuration to identify whether management interfaces are bound to a separate interface and VLAN from storage data interfaces.
how_to_obtain.command: ip addr show && ip route show
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Separate network interfaces visible for management (e.g., eth0 on management VLAN) and data-plane (e.g., eth1 on storage VLAN) with distinct subnets.

how_to_obtain.instruction: On a dedicated NAS appliance such as Synology or QNAP, check network interface bindings via SSH to verify management service binding addresses.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Management services (ports 80, 443, 22, 161) show listening addresses bound to the management interface IP only, not to the data-plane interface IP or 0.0.0.0.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Review NAS network interface configuration in the vendor web management console to verify separate management and data interface assignments.
how_to_obtain.navigation: NAS Admin Console > Network > Network Interface > Verify a dedicated management interface is configured on a separate VLAN from storage data interfaces > Check Management VLAN ID differs from Data VLAN ID.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Two or more distinct network interfaces shown, with management services explicitly bound to the management-only interface on a separate VLAN.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Review network topology diagrams and change management records to confirm a dedicated management network segment was designed and implemented for the NAS.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Network architecture documentation shows a dedicated management VLAN with separate routing and access controls from the storage data-plane VLAN.

typical_values: false (very common; most SMB and mid-market NAS deployments use a single network interface for both management and data access)
true (seen in enterprise deployments with formal network segmentation policies, particularly in regulated industries)

option_description: Indicates whether NAS management interfaces including HTTP/S admin console, SNMP, and SSH are reachable from the same VLAN or subnet used by storage data-plane clients for NFS, SMB, or iSCSI connections, regardless of whether a dedicated OOB management network exists.
security_impact: The Rego policy triggers management_plane_zone_colocation when this is true AND either dedicated_oob_management_network_present is false or acl_restricts_mgmt_access_to_admin_hosts_only is absent. Reachable management interfaces from the data VLAN collapse the management and data trust zones, allowing any storage client to attempt credential brute-force, exploit web admin vulnerabilities, or interact with SNMP from the storage client network position.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Perform port connectivity tests from a storage client host in the data-plane VLAN to NAS management ports to empirically verify reachability.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: All management ports show 'filtered' from the data-plane VLAN source; any 'open' results confirm management interfaces are exposed on the data VLAN.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Check NAS service listening addresses and compare to the data-plane VLAN subnet to determine if management services are bound to data-plane IPs.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Listening addresses for management ports show only management VLAN IPs or loopback; any data-plane VLAN IP in the output confirms management exposure on the data VLAN.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Verify firewall or ACL rules between the data VLAN and NAS management ports to confirm whether inter-VLAN management access is explicitly blocked.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: DROP or REJECT rules blocking management ports from data-plane VLAN source ranges; absence of such rules combined with open listening sockets indicates exposure.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Review NAS SSH and web access logs for authentication attempts sourced from storage client VLAN IP ranges to detect existing access from data-plane hosts.
how_to_obtain.command: grep 'sshd' /var/log/auth.log | awk '{print $11}' | sort | uniq -c | sort -rn | head -20
how_to_obtain.expected_output: SSH authentication events sourced only from management VLAN IPs; any source IPs from storage client subnets confirm management interfaces are reachable from the data VLAN.

typical_values: true (common default; most NAS devices listen on all interfaces by default without explicit management interface binding)
false (achieved through explicit interface binding configuration or firewall rules blocking management ports from data-plane VLAN sources)

option_description: Controls whether network ACLs or firewall rules explicitly restrict access to NAS management interfaces (HTTP/S, SNMP, SSH) exclusively to authorized administrative hosts or management-plane IP ranges, while blocking access from storage data-plane client subnets.
security_impact: The Rego policy for management_plane_zone_colocation fires when acl_restricts_mgmt_access_to_admin_hosts_only is false in combination with either no dedicated OOB management network or management interfaces exposed on the data VLAN. Without this ACL, compromised storage clients can directly reach NAS management consoles, collapsing the management and data trust zones and enabling lateral movement from any storage client to full device administration.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Query the perimeter firewall or switch ACL for rules permitting TCP/443, TCP/80, TCP/22, and UDP/161 toward the NAS management IP, then verify source restrictions match only the admin/management subnet and explicitly deny storage client subnets.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: ACL entries permitting only the management-plane subnet (e.g., 10.0.0.0/24) to reach NAS management ports, with an explicit deny for the storage client subnet (e.g., 10.1.0.0/16).

how_to_obtain.instruction: Log in to the NAS web administration console (e.g., Synology DSM, QNAP QTS, NetApp ONTAP System Manager). Navigate to Control Panel > Security > Firewall or Network > Firewall Rules and review which source IP ranges are permitted on the management port rules.
how_to_obtain.navigation: NAS Admin Console > Control Panel > Security > Firewall / Allowed IP List
how_to_obtain.expected_output: A whitelist containing only the management-plane admin host IPs or subnet, with no entries covering the storage client data-plane subnet.

how_to_obtain.instruction: For Linux-based NAS (e.g., Samba/NFS appliance), inspect iptables or nftables rules to verify management port restrictions are source-IP-scoped to admin hosts only.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Rules showing ACCEPT only for management subnet source IPs on ports 22, 80, 443, 161, with a DROP or REJECT for all other sources including data-plane client ranges.

how_to_obtain.instruction: From a host within the storage client data subnet, attempt to reach the NAS management interface on TCP/443 and TCP/22. Access should be blocked, confirming ACL enforcement is active.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Connection refused or timed out from a storage client subnet host, confirming management ports are not accessible from the data plane.

typical_values: false (management interfaces are accessible from any subnet — very common in SMB and mid-market NAS deployments)
true (ACLs explicitly restrict to a dedicated management VLAN or jump host IP range — common in enterprise and regulated environments)

option_description: Controls whether NAS authentication credentials are validated independently and exclusively within each trust zone, ensuring that a credential valid in one zone cannot be reused in another zone without fresh re-validation at the zone boundary.
security_impact: The Rego policy for shared_credential_propagation_across_zones triggers when credential_scope_isolation_enforced is false alongside more than one zone sharing credentials, or when combined with partial boundary revalidation. Without scope isolation, a credential stolen from a lower-trust zone (e.g., DMZ) can be directly presented to authenticate NAS shares in a higher-trust zone (e.g., production), bypassing zone demarcation controls entirely.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Interview the directory services or storage admin team to determine if NAS share authentication uses a single shared service account across multiple trust zone environments, or whether zone-specific service accounts with distinct credentials are provisioned per zone.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Documentation showing separate service account credentials per trust zone (e.g., svc-nas-dmz@domain.com vs svc-nas-prod@domain.com) with no credential overlap.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Query Active Directory or LDAP to enumerate service accounts with NAS-related SPNs or group memberships and check whether the same account object is used across hosts or shares mapped to different trust zone VLANs.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Distinct service accounts per zone with non-overlapping group memberships; absence of a single account appearing in both DMZ-access and production-access groups.

how_to_obtain.instruction: On Linux-based NAS systems using PAM, inspect PAM configuration and nsswitch to determine if zone-specific PAM stacks or RBAC policies re-challenge credentials at zone ingress points, or if the same auth stack services all zones uniformly.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Separate PAM service configurations per trust zone interface, or access.conf entries restricting specific accounts to specific source host ranges.

how_to_obtain.instruction: If using NetApp ONTAP, query the SVM security settings via REST API to confirm that SVMs mapped to different trust zones use distinct authentication policies and do not share a common service account.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: JSON output listing distinct user accounts per SVM, with no single account appearing on SVMs that span different trust zone classifications.

typical_values: false (single shared service account or domain credential used across all zones — default in most domain-joined NAS deployments)
true (zone-specific service accounts with enforced RBAC/PAM scope isolation — typical in PCI-DSS or HIPAA-scoped environments)

option_description: An enumerated list of trust zone identifiers (e.g., 'dmz', 'internal', 'production', 'development') that authenticate to NAS shares using the same service account or domain credential set, indicating the blast radius of a credential compromise.
security_impact: The Rego policy for shared_credential_propagation_across_zones triggers when the count of shared_credential_zones exceeds one, combined with either disabled credential scope isolation or inadequate boundary revalidation. A list with more than one entry directly demonstrates that a credential stolen from any one of the listed zones could be used to authenticate NAS access in all other listed zones, making this array the primary input for determining cross-zone credential exposure.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Enumerate NAS share mount configurations across all hosts in each trust zone, extract the service account or credential identifier used for each mount, and group mount points by trust zone to identify shared credentials.
how_to_obtain.command: for host in $(cat nas_client_inventory.txt); do ssh $host 'mount | grep -E "(cifs|nfs)" && cat /etc/fstab | grep -E "(cifs|nfs)"'; done
how_to_obtain.expected_output: A mapping of trust zone to credential name; any credential identifier appearing in more than one zone classification should be listed in this array.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Query keytab files or credential caches on NAS client hosts across zones to identify the principal names used for Kerberos-authenticated NAS access and cross-reference them against the zone classification of each host.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Principal names (e.g., svc-nas@DOMAIN.COM) found in keytabs on hosts across multiple trust zones — these zone names should be recorded in the shared_credential_zones array.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Review Windows credential manager exports or domain group policy preferences (GPP) that configure drive mappings to NAS shares, and identify if the same mapped credential identity is deployed in GPOs scoped to different OU/zone structures.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Drive mapping XML showing userName and runAs attributes; identical credential identities appearing in GPOs linked to both production and development/DMZ OUs indicate shared_credential_zones overlap.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Interview the storage and IAM teams to obtain a matrix of NAS service accounts versus trust zones. Request the NAS share authentication policy documentation and cross-reference account names with zone classifications in the CMDB or network segmentation documentation.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: A documented credential-to-zone mapping confirming whether any single credential identity is authorized in more than one named trust zone — populate the array with all zone names sharing a credential.

typical_values: [] (empty — each zone uses distinct credentials; ideal state)
['production', 'development'] (two zones sharing a single service account — common in environments without NAS credential segmentation)
['dmz', 'internal', 'production'] (three or more zones sharing credentials — high-risk configuration frequently seen in organizations using a single domain service account for all NAS mounts)

option_description: Describes the degree to which NAS authentication credentials are re-challenged or re-validated at trust zone boundary crossing points, with values of 'full' (fresh authentication required), 'partial' (some elements re-checked), or 'none' (original credential passed through without re-challenge).
security_impact: The Rego policy for shared_credential_propagation_across_zones fires on a value of 'none' when multiple zones share credentials, and also fires on 'partial' when credential scope isolation is also disabled. A value of 'none' or 'partial' means a credential obtained in a lower-trust zone can traverse the boundary and authenticate in higher-trust zones without interception, fundamentally negating zone demarcation as a security control for NAS access paths.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Interview network security and storage architects to determine whether zone boundary firewalls, proxies, or authentication brokers are configured to intercept and re-challenge NAS authentication requests as they cross zone demarcation points. Request architecture diagrams for storage traffic flows across zone boundaries.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Documentation showing either an authentication broker/proxy at zone boundaries that issues a fresh challenge (full), a token inspection step that validates claims but does not re-issue credentials (partial), or a transparent pass-through (none).

how_to_obtain.instruction: Capture NAS authentication traffic at a zone boundary firewall interface using packet capture to determine whether authentication handshakes terminate at the boundary device or pass through end-to-end from client to NAS without interception.
how_to_obtain.command: tcpdump -i <boundary_interface> -w /tmp/nas_boundary.pcap port 445 or port 2049 or port 389
how_to_obtain.expected_output: If full revalidation is in place, TCP sessions should terminate at the boundary proxy with new sessions initiated toward the NAS. Pass-through TCP sessions from client IP directly to NAS IP indicate 'none' revalidation.

how_to_obtain.instruction: For environments using a PAM or RADIUS-based authentication proxy at zone boundaries, inspect the proxy configuration to determine if it performs full re-authentication (new credential challenge), attribute inspection only (partial), or pass-through.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Configuration blocks showing 'Auth-Type := PAP' with a full credential verification module chain (full), or 'authorize { ... }' blocks that only check group attributes without re-issuing a challenge (partial), or no intercept configuration (none).

how_to_obtain.instruction: If a next-generation firewall (e.g., Palo Alto, Fortinet) is deployed at zone boundaries, review the security policy for NAS traffic to determine if a User-ID or SSL inspection policy enforces re-authentication or if NAS storage protocol traffic is permitted without authentication inspection.
how_to_obtain.navigation: NGFW Management Console > Policies > Security > [NAS Zone Boundary Rule] > Authentication Profile / User-ID Settings
how_to_obtain.expected_output: A security policy rule with an attached authentication profile requiring credential re-entry maps to 'full'; a User-ID lookup without re-challenge maps to 'partial'; no authentication profile on the NAS traffic rule maps to 'none'.

typical_values: none (most common — NAS traffic traverses zone boundaries without any re-authentication step, typical in flat or loosely segmented networks)
partial (occasional in environments with NGFW User-ID mapping but no actual re-challenge)
full (rare — requires an authenticating proxy or NAC at zone demarcation points, seen in high-security or zero-trust architectures)

option_description: Controls whether egress filtering rules (firewall policies, DLP inspection engines, or protocol-aware inspection rules) are actively applied to outbound NAS replication and backup traffic on protocols such as rsync (TCP/873), NDMP (TCP/10000), and vendor-specific snapshot replication channels as they leave the storage zone.
security_impact: The Rego policy for egress_unfiltered_storage_replication_channels fires independently whenever replication_egress_filtering_enabled is false, regardless of other control states. This means unfiltered replication traffic alone is sufficient to trigger the exposure finding. Without egress filtering, an attacker who compromises a NAS or initiates a rogue replication job can exfiltrate bulk data through replication ports that are typically exempted from inspection due to high volume and trusted-service classification assumptions.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Review the egress firewall policy on the storage zone boundary firewall for rules covering rsync (TCP/873), NDMP (TCP/10000), and vendor replication ports. Confirm whether these rules are subject to deep packet inspection or DLP policy, or are permit-any rules without inspection.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Firewall rules showing rsync and NDMP traffic subject to an inspection profile or DLP policy, rather than a bare permit action with no security profile attached.

how_to_obtain.instruction: In the DLP management console (e.g., Symantec DLP, Forcepoint, Microsoft Purview), navigate to the policy list and search for policies covering network storage or backup protocols. Verify that rsync and NDMP port ranges are included in monitored channels and not listed in bypass/exclusion rules.
how_to_obtain.navigation: DLP Management Console > Policies > Network Monitor > Protocol/Port Coverage > Storage/Replication Protocols
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Active DLP detection rules covering TCP/873 and TCP/10000 egress, with no bypass exception for NAS service account source IPs or storage VLAN source ranges.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Inspect the firewall configuration file exported from the boundary device to identify whether replication protocol ports are subject to an outbound security policy or silently permitted without an inspection profile.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Egress rules for TCP/873 and TCP/10000 referencing an 'inspect' or 'content-filter' action; bare ACCEPT rules with no profile indicate filtering is not enabled.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Review firewall or DLP egress logs for outbound flows from the NAS management IP or storage VLAN on replication ports to verify whether these flows generate inspection log entries or flow silently through without generating DLP/inspection events.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Log entries showing replication traffic generating 'inspected' or 'scanned' disposition records; absence of inspection records for these flows confirms filtering is not applied.

typical_values: false (overwhelmingly common — replication and backup ports are nearly universally excluded from DLP and inspection policies in production environments due to performance impact)
true (uncommon — found only in high-security environments where storage replication traffic is routed through inspection proxies or CASB gateways)

option_description: Controls whether NAS replication and backup job configurations enforce a validated allowlist of permitted destination hosts or trust zone CIDR ranges, preventing replication jobs from targeting arbitrary endpoints, external IP addresses, or unapproved zones not in the authorized replication topology.
security_impact: The Rego policy for egress_unfiltered_storage_replication_channels fires independently whenever replication_destination_zone_validation is false, making this a standalone trigger condition. Without destination zone validation, an attacker with access to NAS replication configuration (e.g., via a compromised storage admin credential or NAS management console) can add an arbitrary external destination to an existing replication job and exfiltrate data at full replication bandwidth without triggering DLP alerts.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Log in to the NAS administration console (e.g., Synology DSM Hyper Backup, QNAP Backup Station, NetApp SnapMirror, Dell EMC RecoverPoint). Navigate to replication or backup job configurations and enumerate all configured destination targets. Verify whether destination addresses are restricted to an internal allowlist or whether arbitrary external addresses are accepted.
how_to_obtain.navigation: NAS Admin Console > Backup & Replication > Replication Jobs > [Job] > Destination Settings
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Destination fields populated with internal management IPs or hostnames matching an approved replication topology; absence of any ad-hoc or external IP targets; a platform-level restriction preventing creation of jobs targeting non-allowlisted destinations.

how_to_obtain.instruction: For NetApp ONTAP SnapMirror, query the peer relationship list via CLI to enumerate all configured replication destinations and confirm all peer cluster/vserver IPs fall within approved internal trust zone ranges.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: A list of destination cluster/vserver identifiers all resolving to IPs within the approved internal storage replication zone; any IP in an external or unknown range indicates missing zone validation.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Inspect rsync job configuration files or cron scripts to determine whether destination host parameters are hardcoded to approved internal hosts, or whether rsync targets are variable or user-configurable without validation.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: rsync destination parameters pointing to specific approved hostnames or IP addresses; absence of wildcard, variable, or externally-resolvable destination parameters confirms zone validation is in place.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Review the change management and backup administration procedures to determine whether a formal approval process exists for adding new replication destinations, including zone classification checks, or whether NAS operators can configure replication targets ad-hoc without security review.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: A documented approval workflow requiring security team sign-off for any new replication destination, with evidence of zone classification checks in recent change tickets.

typical_values: false (common in SMB and mid-market environments where NAS replication jobs are configured by backup operators without destination allowlist enforcement)
true (present in enterprise environments using SnapMirror policies with explicit peer allowlists or backup solutions with destination restriction controls)

option_description: Indicates whether replication or backup traffic originating from NAS systems has been explicitly added to DLP bypass lists, trusted-source exclusions, or firewall inspection exemptions, causing content inspection to be skipped for these high-volume storage protocol flows.
security_impact: The Rego policy for egress_unfiltered_storage_replication_channels fires directly and independently when replication_traffic_dlp_exempted is true, as DLP exemption alone constitutes the exposure condition. An active DLP exemption for replication traffic creates a reliable, policy-sanctioned exfiltration path — data moved under the guise of replication or backup protocols bypasses the primary data loss detection layer, making exfiltration via rogue replication jobs invisible to the DLP platform.

how_to_obtain.instruction: In the DLP management console, navigate to the exception or bypass policy list and search for entries referencing NAS IP ranges, storage service accounts, or replication protocol port numbers (TCP/873, TCP/10000). Confirm whether any active exception matches storage zone traffic.
how_to_obtain.navigation: DLP Management Console > System > Exception Rules / Trusted Sources > [Search for NAS subnet or replication ports]
how_to_obtain.expected_output: No active exception entries matching the NAS storage subnet (e.g., 10.5.0.0/24) or replication ports; the presence of any such entry with an 'allow without inspection' disposition confirms the attribute is true.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Inspect the DLP platform configuration export or trusted-hosts file to enumerate all source IP ranges, service account names, or protocol bypass rules configured as exclusions from content inspection.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: No entries in the trusted sources file matching NAS management or storage zone IP ranges; any matching entry confirms replication traffic is DLP-exempted.

how_to_obtain.instruction: On a Linux-based DLP sensor or inspection proxy, check iptables or nftables rules for NOTRACK or ACCEPT rules that bypass connection tracking for replication port traffic from the NAS subnet.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: No NOTRACK or ACCEPT entries matching the NAS subnet on replication ports; presence of NOTRACK rules confirms inspection bypass is active.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Review DLP incident and flow logs for the past 30 days, filtering by source IP in the NAS storage zone. If high-volume replication traffic is present in network flow logs but generates zero DLP scan or policy match records, this confirms an active exemption is in place.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: A significantly higher count of 'bypassed' vs 'inspected' records for NAS source IPs confirms DLP exemption is active; zero DLP records for known-active replication jobs is also conclusive.

typical_values: true (very common — DLP and network inspection teams routinely exempt NAS replication traffic citing performance constraints, large transfer sizes, and trusted-service justifications)
false (less common — seen in environments with dedicated high-throughput DLP inspection appliances or where replication traffic is routed through inline CASB gateways)

option_description: Controls whether the NAS device mandates cryptographic message integrity signing for all SMB connections, configured as 'RequireSecuritySignature = 1' on Windows-based NAS or 'server signing = mandatory' on Samba-based systems, preventing NTLM relay attacks by ensuring SMB messages cannot be silently relayed or modified by a man-in-the-middle at zone boundaries.
security_impact: The Rego policy for smb_relay_path_across_zone_boundary fires when smb_signing_enforced is false in combination with a multi-zone cross-zone authentication scope. Without mandatory SMB signing, the NAS system can serve as an inadvertent NTLM relay point — an attacker positioned at a trust zone boundary can capture SMB authentication challenges from one zone and relay them to authenticate in another zone, using the NAS as a bridge across zone demarcations without possessing the actual credential.

how_to_obtain.instruction: On a Windows Server-based NAS (e.g., Windows Storage Server), check the registry for the SMB server signing requirement. A value of 1 confirms mandatory signing is enforced.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: RequireSecuritySignature    REG_DWORD    0x1  (value of 0x1 = mandatory signing enforced; 0x0 = not enforced)

how_to_obtain.instruction: On Samba-based NAS systems (Linux NAS appliances, FreeNAS/TrueNAS), inspect the smb.conf file for the 'server signing' directive to determine the signing enforcement level.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: A line reading 'server signing = mandatory' confirms enforcement is active. Values of 'auto', 'optional', or 'disabled' confirm signing is not enforced and the attribute should be set to false.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Use the nmap SMB security mode script to remotely enumerate the SMB signing configuration on the NAS target IP to verify signing requirement from a network perspective.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Output showing 'message_signing: required' confirms mandatory SMB signing. Output showing 'message_signing: disabled' or 'message_signing: supported' (but not required) confirms the attribute should be false.

how_to_obtain.instruction: On TrueNAS SCALE/CORE, navigate to the Sharing > Windows Shares (SMB) > Configure SMB Service panel and check the 'Enable SMB2/3 Durable Handles' and signing settings. On Synology DSM, navigate to Control Panel > File Services > SMB > Advanced Settings and verify the 'Signing' option is set to Required.
how_to_obtain.navigation: NAS Admin Console > Control Panel > File Services > SMB > Advanced Settings > Signing = Required
how_to_obtain.expected_output: The signing dropdown or toggle shows 'Required' or 'Mandatory'; any value of 'Disabled', 'Auto', or 'Optional' maps to false for this attribute.

typical_values: false (default in many NAS appliances — SMB signing defaults to 'auto' or 'optional' to maximize client compatibility, including with older clients that do not support signing)
true (enforced in Active Directory-integrated environments where Group Policy sets RequireSecuritySignature, or in hardened NAS configurations following CIS benchmarks)

option_description: Controls whether the perimeter firewall or ACL enforces a deny rule for SMB (TCP 445) and NetBIOS (TCP/UDP 137-139) traffic ingressing the NAS trust zone from untrusted or lower-trust zones, preventing NTLM relay attack vectors.
security_impact: The Rego rule smb_relay_path_across_zone_boundary fires when ntlm_traffic_blocked_at_boundary is false AND cross_zone_authentication_scope is multi_zone. Without this block, an attacker in a lower-trust zone can relay NTLM authentication challenges through the NAS to impersonate legitimate users against higher-trust systems. SMB relay attacks require only network-level access to port 445; the absence of a boundary deny rule is sufficient to expose the path.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Query the perimeter firewall or zone-boundary ACL for rules affecting port 445 and NetBIOS ports on the NAS-facing interface using firewall CLI tools.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Explicit deny entries for TCP 445 and TCP/UDP 137-139 inbound from untrusted zone subnets. Absence of any matching deny rule indicates traffic is permitted.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Perform a TCP connection test from a host in an untrusted zone toward the NAS IP on port 445 to confirm whether the boundary actively blocks the traffic.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: All tested ports should return 'filtered' status. A 'open' or 'closed' response indicates the boundary is not blocking the traffic.

how_to_obtain.instruction: For Linux-based firewalls (iptables/nftables) or pfSense/OPNsense, inspect the ruleset file exported from the zone-boundary device.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: DROP or REJECT rules matching destination port 445 and 137-139 for traffic sourced from untrusted zone CIDRs destined toward the NAS subnet.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Log in to the firewall management console (e.g., Palo Alto Panorama, Fortinet FortiManager, Cisco FMC) and review the zone-boundary policy for rules blocking SMB and NetBIOS from untrusted zones to the NAS zone.
how_to_obtain.navigation: Firewall Admin Console > Policies > Security Rules > Filter by Destination Zone = NAS_Zone > Review rules matching ports 445, 137, 138, 139
how_to_obtain.expected_output: At least one deny/block rule with source zone set to untrusted/external and destination matching the NAS zone, covering ports 445 and 137-139.

typical_values: true
false

option_description: Describes whether the NAS device participates in an authentication context (e.g., Active Directory domain membership, LDAP realm, or credential acceptance) that spans multiple network trust zones, meaning credentials valid in one zone are also honored in another.
security_impact: The Rego rule smb_relay_path_across_zone_boundary triggers when cross_zone_authentication_scope is multi_zone combined with either ntlm_traffic_blocked_at_boundary being false or SMB signing not enforced. A multi-zone authentication scope means stolen or relayed credentials from a lower-trust zone authenticate successfully against the NAS or higher-trust systems, eliminating zone-boundary credential isolation.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Check whether the NAS is domain-joined and identify the domain's reachability across zones using realm or domain membership queries on the NAS host.
how_to_obtain.command: realm list 2>/dev/null || net ads info 2>/dev/null || wbinfo --own-domain
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Output shows the domain name the NAS is joined to. Cross-reference this domain against the network zone topology to determine if domain controllers are accessible from multiple zones.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Review the Samba or SSSD configuration on Linux-based NAS systems to identify which authentication backends and realms are configured.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: If realm or security settings reference a domain reachable from more than one zone, or if multiple auth backends cover different zones, the scope is multi_zone.

how_to_obtain.instruction: On a commercial NAS (Synology, QNAP, NetApp ONTAP), navigate to the directory services or authentication settings page to review domain membership and accepted credential sources.
how_to_obtain.navigation: NAS Admin UI > Control Panel > Domain/LDAP > Review joined domain and allowed client subnets/zones
how_to_obtain.expected_output: If the NAS accepts authentication from clients in more than one defined trust zone (e.g., production and DMZ), the scope is multi_zone.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Interview storage or identity administrators to determine whether service accounts or domain trusts used by the NAS are intentionally or unintentionally accessible from multiple network segments with different trust classifications.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Confirmation that the NAS authentication context is either scoped to a single zone (single_zone) or spans zone boundaries (multi_zone).

typical_values: single_zone
multi_zone

option_description: Specifies the level of iSCSI target access control based on initiator IQN whitelisting: none means open discovery with no IQN restrictions, partial means IQNs are listed but not aligned to trust zone membership, and enforced means IQN restrictions are strictly applied per trust zone.
security_impact: The Rego rule iscsi_initiator_zone_enforcement_gap fires immediately when iscsi_initiator_acl_enforcement is none, and also when it is partial combined with absent or weak_or_static CHAP. Without IQN-based ACLs, any iSCSI initiator reachable at the network level can connect to storage targets regardless of zone membership, allowing unauthorized block-level storage access from lower-trust zones.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Inspect iSCSI target ACL configuration using targetcli on Linux software iSCSI targets to list defined NodeACLs per target.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Each target should list explicit initiator IQNs under the acls section. An empty acls list with attribute 'generate_node_acls=1' or 'authentication=0' indicates 'none'.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Check legacy iscsitarget or LIO configuration files for ACL definitions and open discovery settings.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Presence of explicit initiator IQN allow lists per target. Absence or wildcard entries indicate 'none' or 'partial' enforcement.

how_to_obtain.instruction: On a SAN management console (NetApp System Manager, Dell EMC Unisphere, HPE MSA), navigate to iSCSI target host groups or initiator group settings to review per-target IQN restrictions.
how_to_obtain.navigation: SAN Management Console > Storage > iSCSI > Targets > Select Target > Initiator ACL / Host Group > Review listed IQNs and zone alignment
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Each target should have a defined list of authorized initiator IQNs mapped to specific trust zone host groups. Open or empty lists indicate 'none'.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Query NetApp ONTAP REST API to retrieve iSCSI initiator group definitions and verify zone-aligned IQN membership.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: JSON response listing igroups with initiator IQNs. Empty initiator arrays or igroups lacking zone-specific membership indicate 'none' or 'partial'.

typical_values: none
partial
enforced

option_description: Describes the CHAP mutual authentication configuration on iSCSI targets: absent means CHAP is disabled entirely, weak_or_static means CHAP is enabled but uses shared secrets that are not differentiated per trust zone or are never rotated, and per_zone_rotated means CHAP secrets are unique per zone with a documented rotation schedule.
security_impact: The Rego rule iscsi_initiator_zone_enforcement_gap triggers when iscsi_initiator_acl_enforcement is partial AND chap_authentication_state is absent or weak_or_static. Absent or static CHAP means that even if some IQN filtering exists, a spoofed or enumerated IQN from a lower-trust zone can authenticate to the iSCSI target without cryptographic proof of identity, bypassing the partial ACL control.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Check CHAP configuration on Linux LIO/targetcli iSCSI targets by listing authentication attributes for each target portal group.
how_to_obtain.command: targetcli /iscsi/<target_iqn>/tpg1 get attribute authentication; targetcli /iscsi/<target_iqn>/tpg1/acls/<initiator_iqn> get auth userid password mutual_userid mutual_password
how_to_obtain.expected_output: authentication=1 with non-empty userid/password fields indicates CHAP is present. Identical secrets across multiple ACL entries or never-changed timestamps indicate weak_or_static.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Inspect iSCSI target daemon configuration files for CHAP secret definitions and assess whether secrets are unique per initiator/zone.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Distinct IncomingUser credentials per initiator entry. A single shared credential across all initiators indicates weak_or_static; no credentials indicate absent.

how_to_obtain.instruction: On commercial SAN platforms (NetApp ONTAP, Dell EMC), navigate to iSCSI security settings to verify CHAP configuration and review secret management policies.
how_to_obtain.navigation: SAN Management Console > Protocols > iSCSI > Security > CHAP Configuration > Review per-initiator secrets and rotation policy documentation
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Distinct CHAP secrets per initiator group aligned to trust zones, with a documented rotation schedule. A single global secret or disabled CHAP indicates absent or weak_or_static.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Interview storage administrators to determine whether CHAP secrets are documented in a secrets manager, differentiated per zone, and rotated on a defined schedule.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Confirmation of per-zone unique secrets stored in a vault (e.g., HashiCorp Vault, CyberArk) with rotation evidence. Ad-hoc or undocumented secrets indicate weak_or_static.

typical_values: absent
weak_or_static
per_zone_rotated

option_description: Indicates whether storage LUN masking (host group membership and fabric zoning) is configured such that LUNs presented to hosts in one trust zone are inaccessible to initiators from any other trust zone, enforcing a 1:1 alignment between LUN visibility and trust zone membership.
security_impact: The Rego rule iscsi_initiator_zone_enforcement_gap fires when lun_masking_zone_aligned is false AND iscsi_initiator_acl_enforcement is not enforced. Without zone-aligned LUN masking, even if some IQN filtering is attempted, a compromised host or spoofed initiator from a different zone may still discover and access LUNs intended for a higher-trust zone, enabling direct block-level data access across zone boundaries.

how_to_obtain.instruction: On Linux systems with multipath or iSCSI, enumerate visible LUNs from a test initiator in a lower-trust zone to verify whether LUNs from other zones are discoverable.
how_to_obtain.command: iscsiadm -m discovery -t sendtargets -p <target_ip>:3260 && iscsiadm -m node --login && lsblk -S | grep iscsi
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Only LUNs assigned to the initiator's own trust zone should be visible. LUNs from other zones appearing in the output indicate misaligned masking.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Query NetApp ONTAP or similar array API to retrieve LUN map configurations and cross-reference igroup memberships against zone topology.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Each LUN map entry should associate a LUN with an igroup whose initiators belong exclusively to one trust zone. Cross-zone igroup membership indicates misalignment.

how_to_obtain.instruction: In the SAN management console, review host group or initiator group assignments for all LUNs and map them against the documented zone topology.
how_to_obtain.navigation: SAN Management Console > Storage > LUNs > LUN Mapping > For each LUN, review Host Group > Compare host IQNs against trust zone membership registry
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Each LUN's host group contains only initiators from the same defined trust zone. Any host group with members from multiple zones indicates false alignment.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Review Fibre Channel or iSCSI zone configuration files exported from the SAN fabric switch to verify hard zoning aligns with trust zone boundaries.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Zone definitions contain only initiator-target pairs from the same trust zone. Mixed-zone zone members indicate misaligned LUN masking.

typical_values: true
false

option_description: Controls whether flow telemetry (NetFlow, sFlow, IPFIX, or equivalent) is collected for east-west traffic within the storage VLAN or zone, capturing peer-to-peer and client-to-NAS communications that do not traverse inter-zone boundaries and thus bypass perimeter monitoring.
security_impact: The Rego rule insufficient_east_west_monitoring_on_storage_vlan triggers when intra_zone_flow_logging_enabled is false (independently). Lateral movement between storage clients within the same zone—such as unauthorized SMB access, port scanning, or data staging—is entirely invisible to perimeter-facing controls. Flow logging of intra-zone traffic is the baseline visibility control required to detect these patterns before they escalate.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Check NetFlow or sFlow export configuration on the storage VLAN switch to confirm intra-VLAN sampling is enabled, including switched traffic that does not exit the VLAN.
how_to_obtain.command: show flow exporter | grep -A 5 'storage\|NAS\|VLAN' 2>/dev/null || show sflow
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Flow exporter configuration referencing the storage VLAN interface with an active collector destination and sampling rate. Absence indicates flow logging is not enabled for that segment.

how_to_obtain.instruction: On Linux-based routers or switches running softflowd or pmacctd, inspect the daemon configuration for the storage interface or VLAN.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Configuration entries referencing the storage VLAN interface (e.g., eth1.100 or bond0.200) confirming flow capture is active for that segment.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Query the SIEM or flow collector for intra-zone storage VLAN flow records within the last 24 hours to confirm data is actively arriving from the storage segment.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Flow records showing source and destination IPs both within the storage VLAN subnet. Zero records indicate either no intra-zone flows or flow logging is absent.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Review the network monitoring platform (e.g., SolarWinds NTA, Elastic, ntopng) for flow data sources and verify the storage VLAN is listed as an active exporter.
how_to_obtain.navigation: Flow Collector Dashboard > Data Sources > Exporters > Verify storage VLAN switch IP is listed > Review last-received timestamp and intra-VLAN traffic volume
how_to_obtain.expected_output: An active exporter entry for the storage VLAN switch with recent timestamps and non-zero intra-zone flow records.

typical_values: true
false

option_description: Indicates whether an IDS, NDR (Network Detection and Response), or behavioral analytics platform has sensors deployed within the storage VLAN or zone and is configured with active alerting policies targeting storage protocol anomalies such as unusual access volumes, lateral movement indicators, or protocol-level abuse.
security_impact: The Rego rule insufficient_east_west_monitoring_on_storage_vlan triggers when anomaly_detection_applied_to_storage_zone is false (independently). Even when flow logging is present, it provides raw telemetry without behavioral analysis. Without active anomaly detection, ransomware staging, unauthorized mass data access, or protocol-level scanning within the storage zone will not generate alerts, allowing attackers extended dwell time within the zone boundary.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Review the NDR or IDS management console to confirm sensor placement covers the storage VLAN and that active detection policies for storage protocols (SMB, NFS, iSCSI) are enabled.
how_to_obtain.navigation: NDR/IDS Console (e.g., Darktrace, ExtraHop, Suricata) > Sensors/Probes > Verify sensor assigned to storage VLAN interface > Detection Policies > Confirm SMB, NFS, iSCSI anomaly rules are active and alerting
how_to_obtain.expected_output: At least one sensor covering the storage VLAN with enabled rule sets for storage protocol anomalies and confirmed alert generation in the past reporting period.

how_to_obtain.instruction: On a Suricata-based IDS, verify that storage-zone interface capture and relevant rule sets are active and producing alerts.
how_to_obtain.command: suricata-update list-enabled-sources | grep -i storage; grep -E '(interface|af-packet)' /etc/suricata/suricata.yaml | grep -i <storage_vlan_interface>
how_to_obtain.expected_output: The storage VLAN interface listed under af-packet or pcap capture configuration, with SMB/NFS ruleset sources enabled.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Check the SIEM for alerts generated by the anomaly detection system that reference source or destination IPs within the storage VLAN subnet over the past 30 days.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Alert entries referencing storage VLAN IPs. Complete absence of any alerts—even informational—over 30 days may indicate the sensor is not positioned in the storage zone.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Interview the SOC or network security team to confirm whether the storage VLAN is in scope for anomaly detection and whether alerts from that zone have been actioned recently.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Confirmation that the storage VLAN is explicitly listed in sensor coverage documentation and that recent triage records exist for storage zone alerts.

typical_values: true
false

option_description: Indicates whether any NAS share or export is configured to permit unauthenticated access, including SMB guest shares (guest ok = yes), NFS exports with world-readable permissions combined with no_root_squash or all_squash with guest UID mapping, or AFP shares with guest access enabled.
security_impact: The Rego rule guest_or_anonymous_share_exposure_at_zone_edge triggers when anonymous_or_guest_access_enabled is true AND zone boundary ingress filtering for storage protocols is absent AND the NAS is reachable from an untrusted or adjacent zone. Anonymous access eliminates the authentication requirement entirely; any host that can reach the NAS network port can read or write share data without credentials, making it the highest-impact misconfiguration for zone-edge NAS deployments.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Inspect the Samba configuration file for shares with guest ok or public settings enabled.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: 'guest ok = yes' or 'public = yes' entries under any share definition indicate anonymous SMB access is enabled. Clean output (no matches) suggests it is disabled.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Review NFS exports configuration for world-readable or guest-mapped exports, especially those combining all_squash with a low-privilege or guest UID.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Exports with '*(rw)', '*(ro)', 'all_squash,anonuid=65534', or no_root_squash combined with a world-accessible CIDR indicate guest-equivalent access. Exports restricted to specific authorized host CIDRs with root_squash are acceptable.

how_to_obtain.instruction: On Synology DSM, QNAP QTS, or TrueNAS, navigate to share management and review the permissions and access controls for each defined share.
how_to_obtain.navigation: NAS Admin UI > File Services > SMB/NFS/AFP Shares > For each share, review Access Control > Check for 'Allow guest access', 'Everyone' group permissions, or anonymous user entries
how_to_obtain.expected_output: No shares should have guest access enabled or 'Everyone' listed with read/write permissions. Any such entry confirms anonymous_or_guest_access_enabled = true.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Attempt an unauthenticated SMB connection to the NAS from a test host to confirm whether guest sessions are accepted without credentials.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: A successful share listing returned without prompting for credentials indicates guest SMB access is active. An 'NT_STATUS_LOGON_FAILURE' or authentication prompt indicates guest access is disabled.

typical_values: true
false

option_description: Controls whether the network zone boundary enforcement point (firewall, ACL, or security group) contains explicit ingress deny or drop rules that prevent unauthenticated storage protocol traffic — specifically SMB (TCP/445), NFS (TCP/UDP 2049), AFP (TCP/548), and iSCSI (TCP/3260) — from entering the storage zone when originating from adjacent or untrusted network zones such as DMZs, guest VLANs, or partner network segments.
security_impact: This attribute is a direct input to the `guest_or_anonymous_share_exposure_at_zone_edge` Rego rule, which fires when `anonymous_or_guest_access_enabled` is true, `reachable_from_untrusted_or_adjacent_zone` is true, AND this attribute evaluates to false (no blocking ingress filter). Without these boundary-level deny rules, even NAS systems with host-level share restrictions can be reached by unauthenticated clients from untrusted zones, creating a missing_control exposure. The absence of per-protocol ACLs at the zone boundary firewall also feeds the broader `permissive_storage_protocol_ingress_filtering` exposure, which can trigger when `storage_protocol_zone_acls_configured` is false alongside observed unauthorized access. A false value here means the NAS storage zone is effectively unguarded at the perimeter against unauthenticated protocol initiation, allowing SMB relay, anonymous share enumeration, and NFS mount attempts from lower-trust zones.

how_to_obtain.instruction: On a Linux-based or pfSense/OPNsense firewall, dump the active ruleset and search for explicit deny or reject rules targeting storage protocol ports from untrusted source zones. Verify rules exist for TCP/445, TCP/UDP 2049, TCP/548, and TCP/3260 with untrusted or adjacent zone source prefixes.
how_to_obtain.command: iptables -L FORWARD -n -v --line-numbers | grep -E '(445|2049|548|3260)'; ip6tables -L FORWARD -n -v --line-numbers | grep -E '(445|2049|548|3260)'
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Output shows DROP or REJECT rules for dports 445, 2049, 548, and 3260 with source addresses matching untrusted/adjacent zone CIDRs. Missing output for any of these ports indicates the control is absent (false).

how_to_obtain.instruction: For Cisco IOS/IOS-XE firewalls or layer-3 switches acting as zone boundary enforcement, review the ACL entries applied to the interface facing untrusted zones. Confirm deny statements exist for each storage protocol port.
how_to_obtain.command: show ip access-lists | include -A (445|2049|548|3260); show running-config | section ip access-list
how_to_obtain.expected_output: ACL entries containing 'deny tcp [untrusted-CIDR] any eq 445', 'deny tcp any any eq 2049', and equivalent entries for 548 and 3260 applied to the inbound interface of the untrusted/adjacent zone. Absence of any of these constitutes a false value.

how_to_obtain.instruction: In AWS, navigate to the VPC Security Groups or Network ACLs associated with the storage subnet. Review inbound rules to confirm explicit deny entries (NACLs) or absence of allow entries (Security Groups) for ports 445, 2049, 548, and 3260 sourced from untrusted or DMZ CIDR ranges.
how_to_obtain.navigation: AWS Console → VPC → Security Groups → [Storage-Zone-SG] → Inbound Rules; OR VPC → Network ACLs → [Storage-Subnet-NACL] → Inbound Rules → filter by port 445/2049/548/3260
how_to_obtain.expected_output: No inbound allow rules permitting 0.0.0.0/0 or untrusted-zone CIDRs on ports 445, 2049, 548, or 3260. For NACLs, explicit DENY rules with lower rule numbers than any ALLOW for these ports from untrusted sources confirms the control is true.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Inspect the firewall or ACL configuration file on the boundary device directly. Search for explicit deny or drop statements referencing storage protocol ports applied to interfaces or zones associated with the untrusted-to-storage-zone traffic path.
how_to_obtain.file_path: /etc/firewall/rules.conf, /etc/pf.conf, /etc/iptables/rules.v4, or vendor-specific paths such as /config/active/firewall (Juniper SRX flat config)
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Configuration lines containing block/deny/drop actions targeting destination ports 445, 2049, 548, and 3260 with source matching untrusted zone subnets. A clean grep result with no output indicates the control is false.

typical_values: false (common in flat network deployments where NAS is on a shared VLAN with workstations and no zone boundary firewall exists)
false (observed in cloud environments where Security Groups only define allow rules and rely on implicit deny, but no NACLs explicitly block storage ports from peered or adjacent subnets)
true (enforced in PCI-DSS or HIPAA environments with dedicated storage VLANs and explicit perimeter ACLs blocking all storage protocols from non-authorized source zones)
true (enforced via cloud-native NACL deny rules on storage subnets in environments with defined DMZ or partner peering zones)

option_description: Indicates the observed network reachability state of the NAS system's storage protocol ports (SMB/445, NFS/2049, AFP/548, iSCSI/3260) from hosts located in untrusted or adjacent network zones such as DMZ segments, guest VLANs, partner interconnects, or other lower-trust network boundaries. A true value means a host in those zones can successfully initiate a TCP or UDP connection to the NAS on these ports, regardless of whether authentication ultimately succeeds.
security_impact: This attribute is the third required condition in the `guest_or_anonymous_share_exposure_at_zone_edge` Rego rule, which triggers a missing_control exposure when this is true alongside enabled anonymous/guest access and absent ingress filters. Network reachability from untrusted zones is the foundational precondition for all NAS-based attacks: without it, SMB relay, NFS mount enumeration, anonymous share browsing, and iSCSI LUN discovery attacks cannot be initiated. When true, this value confirms that boundary controls — whether firewalls, security groups, or ACLs — are either absent or misconfigured, enabling cross-zone storage session initiation. Even if `zone_boundary_ingress_filter_blocks_storage_protocols` is claimed to be true, a true value here empirically demonstrates that the ingress filter is ineffective, overridden, or applied to the wrong interface. This makes it a critical verification attribute for confirming actual exposure rather than relying solely on ruleset inspection.

how_to_obtain.instruction: From a host or jump server located in the untrusted or adjacent zone (e.g., a DMZ instance, guest VLAN host, or partner-network VM), perform a TCP port scan against the NAS management or data IP address targeting storage protocol ports. A successful SYN-ACK or open port response confirms reachability is true.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Nmap reports '445/tcp open microsoft-ds', '2049/tcp open nfs', or similar for any of the four ports. Any 'open' result from an untrusted zone host confirms reachable_from_untrusted_or_adjacent_zone = true. All ports reporting 'filtered' or 'closed' with no RST (dropped by firewall) supports false.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Review routing tables and firewall state tables on the boundary device to determine whether a forwarding path exists between untrusted zone source addresses and the NAS IP on storage protocol destination ports. Check for established or permitted sessions in the connection state table.
how_to_obtain.command: netstat -an | grep -E ':(445|2049|548|3260).*ESTABLISHED'; conntrack -L | grep -E 'dport=(445|2049|548|3260)'; show conn | include <NAS_IP> (ASA/FTD CLI)
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Active or recent ESTABLISHED connections to NAS IP on storage ports originating from untrusted CIDR ranges in the state table confirms true. Empty results or only connections from authorized storage-zone hosts supports false.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Query firewall flow logs, NetFlow/IPFIX records, or cloud VPC flow logs for connection attempts to the NAS IP on storage protocol ports originating from untrusted or adjacent zone source IPs. Successful flows (accepted action, non-zero bytes) confirm reachability.
how_to_obtain.command: grep -E 'ACCEPT|ALLOW' /var/log/firewall.log | grep -E '(445|2049|548|3260)' | grep <NAS_IP>; aws logs filter-log-events --log-group-name <VPC-Flow-Log-Group> --filter-pattern '{$.dstPort = 445 && $.action = ACCEPT && $.dstAddr = <NAS_IP>}'
how_to_obtain.file_path: /var/log/firewall.log, /var/log/ufw.log, or cloud provider flow log storage (S3 bucket or CloudWatch Logs)
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Log entries showing ACCEPT/ALLOW action for destination ports 445, 2049, 548, or 3260 targeting the NAS IP from source IPs in untrusted zone CIDRs confirms true. Log entries showing only REJECT/DROP for these port/source combinations supports false.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Use cloud provider APIs to programmatically evaluate the effective network path between an untrusted zone resource and the NAS. AWS Reachability Analyzer, Azure Network Watcher, and GCP Connectivity Tests can determine whether packets can traverse zone boundaries to reach storage ports.
how_to_obtain.command: aws ec2 create-network-insights-path --source <untrusted-zone-instance-id> --destination <nas-instance-id> --protocol tcp --destination-port 445; aws ec2 start-network-insights-analysis --network-insights-path-id <path-id>; aws ec2 describe-network-insights-analyses --network-insights-analysis-ids <analysis-id>
how_to_obtain.navigation: AWS Console → VPC → Reachability Analyzer → Create and analyze path from untrusted-zone ENI to NAS ENI on port 445/2049/548/3260; Azure Portal → Network Watcher → Connection Troubleshoot → specify source VM in DMZ and destination NAS IP with port
how_to_obtain.expected_output: API response with 'NetworkPathFound: true' or Reachability Analyzer status 'reachable' confirms reachable_from_untrusted_or_adjacent_zone = true. 'NetworkPathFound: false' or 'not-reachable' with an identified blocking component (Security Group, NACL, Route Table) supports false.

typical_values: true (frequently observed in environments where NAS is deployed on a flat corporate LAN shared with workstations, IoT devices, and guest WiFi bridged to the same broadcast domain)
true (observed in legacy data centers where storage VLAN trunking is overly permissive and inter-VLAN routing via a core switch lacks ACLs blocking storage ports)

false (correctly configured in environments with dedicated storage VLANs, zone-based firewalls enforcing micro-segmentation, and cloud security groups scoped to authorized storage client CIDR blocks only)

true (common in cloud environments where NAS EC2 instances or EFS mount targets are placed in public or shared subnets without NACLs, or where Security Group rules allow 0.0.0.0/0 on NFS/SMB ports for convenience)
